title: Plus One
directAnswer: The array is a big integer, one digit per slot, most-significant first. To add one, walk from the RIGHT simulating grade-school addition with a carry. If a digit is less than 9, increment it and you're done — there's no carry to propagate. If it's 9, set it to 0 and continue left. The only case that grows the array is all 9s (e.g. 999 → 1000): after the loop a carry remains, so prepend a leading 1.

remember.pattern: Grade-school addition with carry, scanning right-to-left
remember.formula:
for i from last index down to 0:
    if digits[i] < 9:
        digits[i] += 1
        return digits      # no carry → done early
    digits[i] = 0          # 9 + 1 = 10 → write 0, carry on
# fell off the left edge → was all 9s
return [1] + digits        # prepend the leading 1
rules: Iterate from the **last index toward 0** — addition carries from least-significant to most-significant, i.e. right to left.
If `digits[i] < 9`, **increment and return immediately** — a non-9 absorbs the +1 and stops any carry.
If `digits[i] == 9`, set it to **0 and continue** left; the carry keeps rippling through consecutive 9s.
Only the **all-9s case** (`999 → 1000`) survives the loop — then prepend a leading **1**, growing the array by one.
There is **at most one** carry to propagate (you add exactly 1), so a single pass suffices — no nested logic.
Don't convert to an int and back: the input can exceed 64-bit range, so digit-by-digit is the safe approach.
whenToUse: A number is represented as an array/list of digits and you must do arithmetic on it
Big-integer addition where the value can overflow native 64-bit types
Any 'increment with carry propagation' over a positional representation
The +1 / +k must ripple through trailing boundary values (9s, or base-b max digits)
antiSignals: The number fits comfortably in a 32/64-bit int → just parse, add, and re-split (but rarely what's asked)
You must add two arbitrary multi-digit arrays → that's Add Strings / Add Two Numbers, a fuller carry loop
Digits are in least-significant-first order → reverse your iteration direction
Non-decimal base or arbitrary increment → generalize the carry, don't hard-code 9 and 1
remember.takeaway: Plus One is the simplest carry-propagation problem: add one to a digit array and let the carry ripple through trailing 9s. The single insight — only all-9s grows the array — and the early-return-on-non-9 trick generalize directly to Add Strings, Add Two Numbers, and Add Binary. Master the right-to-left carry walk here and those become routine.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you simulate positional addition with a carry instead of converting the array to a native integer (which overflows for large inputs), and whether you correctly handle carry propagation through trailing 9s — especially the array-growing all-9s case.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Joining digits into an int, adding 1, and splitting back — silently breaks once the number exceeds 64 bits. Or mishandling 999 → 1000 by forgetting to prepend the new leading digit.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note up front that the array can represent a number too big for a long, so digit-by-digit carry is the robust approach. Mention the early return when a digit < 9 (no carry to propagate) and that only all-9s grows the array length.

problemStatement:
You are given a **large integer** represented as an integer array `digits`, where each `digits[i]` is the `iᵗʰ` digit of the integer. The digits are ordered from **most significant to least significant** in left-to-right order. The large integer does not contain any leading 0's.

Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array of digits.
constraints: digits does not contain any leading 0's
understanding: The array IS a number, one digit per cell, big-endian (digits[0] is the most significant). 'Plus one' means add 1 to that number and return the new digit array. The work is grade-school addition: start at the rightmost digit, carry left through any 9s, and grow the array only if every digit was 9.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the digits most-significant first or least-significant first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Most significant first — digits[0] is the leading digit. So I add starting from the END of the array and carry toward the front.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the number be larger than a 64-bit integer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — up to 100 digits. That's why I won't parse it into a long; I'll do digit-by-digit addition to avoid overflow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there leading zeros, or can the input be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No leading zeros, and length ≥ 1. So [0] represents 0, but I'll never see [0, 5]. The only zero I create is internal carry handling.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I modify the input array or return a new one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I can increment in place for the common case and return the same array; only the all-9s case needs a brand-new, longer array with a leading 1.

examples.explanation: 123 + 1 = 124. The last digit 3 < 9, so just increment it; no carry.
129 + 1 = 130. The 9 becomes 0 and carries; the 2 becomes 3 and stops the carry.
999 + 1 = 1000. Every digit is 9 → all become 0, carry survives the loop → prepend a leading 1, array grows by one.

diagrams.caption: Walk right-to-left. A digit < 9 stops the carry early; consecutive 9s ripple; all-9s grows the array.

approaches.name: Digit-by-Digit Carry (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — and essentially the only correct one for large inputs. Frame it as 'grade-school addition with a carry, scanning right to left'.

complexity.space: O(1) in place, O(n) only when the array grows

hints: The array is a number written one digit per slot, most significant first. How did you add 1 to a number by hand in grade school? Which end did you start from?
Start at the LAST index. If that digit is less than 9, just add 1 and you're finished — there's no carry. Return right away.
If the digit is 9, adding 1 makes it 10: write a 0 and carry the 1 to the left. Keep going. If you run off the left end, every digit was 9 — prepend a leading 1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass from right to left touches each of the n digits at most once → O(n). It mutates in place, so O(1) extra space; the only allocation is the new (n+1)-length array in the all-9s case, which is O(n) and rare.
approaches.explanation:
Read the array as a positional number and replay long-hand addition. The +1 enters at the least-significant digit (the rightmost slot), and a carry only ever moves leftward, so the loop walks from `digits.length - 1` down to `0`.

**Why a digit less than 9 ends everything.** When `digits[i] < 9`, adding one produces a value in `0..9` — a single digit, no overflow into the next place. So you increment that slot and return immediately. Crucially, all digits to its left are untouched and correct, which is why the early return is not just an optimization but the natural stopping point: there is no carry left to propagate.

**Why a 9 turns into a 0 and keeps going.** `9 + 1 = 10`. In positional notation that's a `0` in the current place and a `1` carried to the next more-significant place. So we set `digits[i] = 0` and continue the loop to apply that carry to `digits[i-1]`. Consecutive 9s create a ripple: each becomes 0 and hands the carry left until it finally meets a digit below 9 that absorbs it (the early return above).

**Why only all-9s grows the array.** If every digit is a 9, the carry never finds a digit to absorb it — the loop sets each to 0 and falls off the left edge with a pending carry. That pending carry is a brand-new most-significant digit. `999 + 1 = 1000` needs four slots for a three-slot input, so we allocate a fresh array of length `n + 1`, place a `1` at the front, and leave the rest as the zeros we just wrote. This is the one and only case where the length changes.

**Why we don't parse to an integer.** A tempting shortcut is `Long.parseLong(join(digits)) + 1` then split back. With up to 100 digits, the value vastly exceeds 64-bit range and silently overflows. Digit-by-digit addition sidesteps overflow entirely and is the reason this 'easy' problem is really a big-integer arithmetic check.
approaches.insight: The whole problem hinges on one observation: adding 1 produces at most a single carry, and that carry dies the instant it meets any digit below 9. So the common case is O(1) work (increment the last digit and return), and the worst case (all 9s) is the only time the array grows. Recognizing 'carry stops at the first non-max digit' is what makes the early return obvious.

dryRun.intro: Walk from the rightmost index. A 9 becomes 0 and carries; the first digit < 9 absorbs the carry and we return.

java.explanation: Start at the least-significant digit; the carry only moves left.
A non-9 absorbs the +1 with no carry — this is the early-exit case.
Increment and return immediately; everything to the left is already correct.
9 + 1 = 10 → write 0 here and let the loop carry the 1 leftward.
Only reached for all-9s: allocate one longer array and set the leading 1; the rest stay 0.

python.explanation: Iterate from the last index down to 0 — right to left.
Non-9 stops the carry; increment and return.
Turn a 9 into 0 and continue the loop to apply the carry.
All-9s case: prepend the new leading 1 to the now all-zeros array.

diagrams.title: Carry ripple on [1, 2, 9]
diagrams.caption: The pointer moves right to left; the 9 zeroes out and carries, the 2 absorbs it.

edgeCases.behavior: Single 9 → set to 0, loop ends, return [1, 0]. Smallest array-growing case.
All become 0, carry survives → return [1, 0, 0, 0], length grows from 3 to 4.
Last digit 1 < 9 → increment to 2, return [4, 3, 2, 2]; no carry, O(1) work.

pitfalls: Iterating left to right — the carry direction is wrong; addition carries from least to most significant.
Forgetting the all-9s case, returning an array of zeros without the leading 1.
Parsing the digits into an int/long and adding — overflows for inputs beyond 64-bit range.

commonMistakes: Converting the digit array to a native integer, adding 1, and splitting back — overflows on large inputs.
Forgetting to prepend the leading 1 in the all-9s case (999 → returns [0,0,0] instead of [1,0,0,0]).
Scanning left-to-right and trying to carry rightward — the opposite of how positional addition works.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Parsing to an integer (overflow)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With up to 100 digits the number far exceeds long range, so parse-add-split silently produces garbage or throws. Digit-by-digit addition is overflow-proof.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the all-9s array growth
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only mutate in place and return the same array, [9,9,9] becomes [0,0,0] — the carry off the left edge is dropped. The result must be one slot longer with a leading 1.

followupVariations.hint: Same +1 carry, but on a linked list — reverse, add, reverse back, or use recursion to carry from the tail.

patternNote: Grade-school carry propagation over a positional digit representation. Add one from the right, ripple the carry through trailing 9s, and grow the array only when every digit is 9. The same right-to-left carry loop powers Add Binary, Add Strings, and Add Two Numbers.
